concept.body: Inverse trig turns a known ratio back into its angle. Steps: identify your two known sides relative to the target angle; form the ratio in the correct order (hypotenuse on the bottom for sine and cosine); apply the matching inverse — sin⁻¹ for opp/hyp, cos⁻¹ for adj/hyp, tan⁻¹ for opp/adj. The result is an ANGLE in degrees.

explanationVariants: sin θ = 0.5, so θ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30° — the special angle from Chapter 1.
The angle whose sine is one-half is 30° (short leg = half the hypotenuse).

commonErrors.feedback: 60° is the angle whose COSINE is 0.5 — the complement. The sine of 30° is 0.5.
0.5 is the ratio you started with. Apply sin⁻¹ to get the angle: 30°.

steps.body: Trig so far: angle in, ratio out. Inverse trig runs it backwards: **ratio in, angle out.** If sin θ = 0.28, then θ = sin⁻¹(0.28) ≈ 16.26°. The ⁻¹ isn't an exponent — it means “the angle whose sine is.” Each ratio has its own inverse: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹.

widget.prompt: tan⁻¹(1) asks exactly one question: which angle has a tangent of 1? Hunt it — drag until the opp/adj card reads 1.000. The angle you land on IS what the inverse hands back.
widget.scaleFeedback: Resize the triangle before checking. An inverse takes a ratio and returns an angle; whether the triangle's size is part of that question is worth settling by hand.
widget.successFeedback: 45°, so tan⁻¹(1) = 45° — and you found it the way the inverse does, by hunting the angle whose ratio matches. Watch what the resizes did to the answer: nothing. The inverse is fed a ratio, never a length, which is why it can return an angle at all.
widget.lowFeedback: opp/adj is still under 1.000 — the opposite side is shorter than the adjacent one, which puts the angle below 45°. Open it.
widget.highFeedback: opp/adj has gone past 1.000 — opposite is now longer than adjacent, so the angle is above 45°. Close it back.

predict.reveal: An angle. Forward tangent runs angle → ratio; the inverse runs ratio → angle. Notice what is missing from both directions: any length. That is why resizing the triangle in a moment will change nothing.

steps.body: The workflow: read the two sides you know, form their ratio, then apply the matching inverse. Opposite 7, hypotenuse 25 → opposite/hypotenuse is sine's pair → θ = sin⁻¹(7/25) = sin⁻¹(0.28) ≈ 16.26°. Answer in DEGREES: an inverse hands back an angle, never a bare ratio.

explanationVariants: The sides 7 and 25 are sine's pair; sin⁻¹(7/25) ≈ 16.26°.

widget.prompt: Right triangle: the side opposite θ is 7, the hypotenuse is 25. Find θ in degrees (2 decimals).

commonErrors.feedback: 73.74° = cos⁻¹(7/25) — the OTHER acute angle. For 7 as the opposite side, use sin⁻¹: ≈ 16.26°.
0.28 is the RATIO, not the angle. Finish with the inverse: sin⁻¹(0.28) ≈ 16.26°.
16.7° misreads the calculator — sin⁻¹(0.28) lands at 16.26°. Recheck degree mode and the keys.

explanationVariants: Legs only means tangent: θ = tan⁻¹(5/8) ≈ 32.01°.
Opposite 5 over adjacent 8 is tangent's pair; tan⁻¹(0.625) ≈ 32.01°.

widget.prompt: Legs 5 and 8; θ is the angle OPPOSITE the leg of length 5. Find θ in degrees (2 decimals).

commonErrors.feedback: 57.99° = tan⁻¹(8/5) is the angle opposite the 8. Your angle faces the 5: tan⁻¹(5/8) ≈ 32.01°.
38.68° = sin⁻¹(5/8) treats the 8 as the hypotenuse — but both are LEGS. Use tan⁻¹(5/8) ≈ 32.01°.

steps.body: The two acute angles are partners: they sum to 90°. Find one and the other is free — 90° minus it. That's also your error alarm: cos⁻¹ where sin⁻¹ belonged returns the PARTNER angle, off by exactly the complement. When an answer looks suspiciously like 90° minus what you expected, that's what happened.

widget.prompt: One acute angle of a right triangle is 32.01°. What is the other acute angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 147.99 = 180 − 32.01 spends the whole triangle — but the right angle already claims 90°. Acute pair: 90 − 32.01 = 57.99°.
The two acute angles only match in the 45-45-90 case. Here: 90 − 32.01 = 57.99°.

explanationVariants: Adjacent and hypotenuse are cosine's sides, so cos⁻¹ recovers the angle.
Given adj and hyp, form adj/hyp and undo it with cos⁻¹.

widget.prompt: You know a triangle's ADJACENT leg and its HYPOTENUSE. Which inverse finds the angle?

options.label: cos⁻¹(adjacent ÷ hypotenuse)
options.feedback: Adjacent/hypotenuse is cosine, so its inverse hands back the angle.

options.label: sin⁻¹(adjacent ÷ hypotenuse)
options.feedback: sin⁻¹ expects OPPOSITE/hypotenuse — feeding it adj/hyp returns the complement, the wrong acute angle.

options.label: tan⁻¹(adjacent ÷ hypotenuse)
options.feedback: Tangent's pair is the two LEGS; the hypotenuse never appears in it. This pair belongs to cosine.

options.label: cos⁻¹(hypotenuse ÷ adjacent)
options.feedback: hyp/adj exceeds 1, and no cosine reaches above 1 — the calculator errors. Keep the hypotenuse on the bottom: cos⁻¹(adj/hyp).

hints: The rise (1.2 m) is opposite the ramp angle; the run (6.4 m) is adjacent — two legs.
θ = tan⁻¹(0.1875) — answer in degrees, 2 decimals.
explanationVariants: Rise over run is the tangent; inverting 0.1875 as an angle gives ≈ 10.62°.

widget.prompt: A ramp rises 1.2 m over a horizontal run of 6.4 m. Find its angle with the ground, in degrees (2 decimals).

commonErrors.feedback: 10.81° = sin⁻¹(1.2/6.4) treats the 6.4 m RUN as the sloped surface — it's the horizontal leg. tan⁻¹ gives ≈ 10.62°.
79.38° = tan⁻¹(6.4/1.2) is the ramp's OTHER angle, up at the top. The ground angle is tan⁻¹(1.2/6.4) ≈ 10.62°.
0.19 rounds the RATIO 0.1875 — the tangent, not the angle. Apply tan⁻¹: ≈ 10.62°.

takeaways: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ each undo their ratio: feed the ratio, receive the angle.
Match the inverse to the side pair you actually have — legs only means tan⁻¹.
Acute angles sum to 90°: one inverse computation unlocks both.
steps.teaser: Next: put sides and angles together and solve a right triangle COMPLETELY.
